campaign_epoch.note: Campaign Day 1 — the game's official start date. Subtract this from any party's current date to get days elapsed.

inspirations.religion: Mostly set up like the Greek pantheon but with a few twists. The gods are more active and present in the world, but they don't necessarily intervene directly in mortal affairs. They have specific domains and philosophies that influence their followers, but they more often than not don't demand worship or obedience. Names are heavily influenced by Gaulic and Saxon names.
inspirations.cities: Each major city should have a relatively distinct climate and culture inspired by a mix of real-world cultures but avoid the obvious ones. They need defined demographics, governments, economies, and something that sets them apart.
inspirations.continents: Two continents are known: Kaemahz and Yetgrese. Other continents may exist but are speculative — only these two have any established information. Kaemahz is the primary fantasy-familiar continent; Yetgrese is deliberately unusual with no standard city structures.

continents.name: Kaemahz
continents.flair: The familiar face of the known world — but the familiarity is deceptive. Seven regions each feel like different countries: tribal shamanism in one, collapsed empire in another, question-free banking in the desert, maritime dual-culture on the northeast coast. Travel across Kaemahz is cultural border-crossing as much as geographical.

calendar_system.notes: The 8 day weeks leave 4 days leftover, which is called the Spring Festival halfweek. This is regionally celebrated as a time of renewal and community gathering, with various local traditions. The Spring Festival halfweek is not considered part of any season, but rather a transition period between Winter and Spring.

continents.description: Large continental landmass divided into seven regions. The primary fantasy-familiar continent of the known world — fulfills traditional tropes of kingdoms, trade routes, and established civilizations. Dragonborn presence is strong throughout, particularly concentrated in the southern regions.

notable_features.name: Inkaba
notable_features.notes: Active but not constantly erupting. Located roughly in the center of Kaemahz, east of Cindermarch. Visible from the fortress on clear days. Name means 'navel' (Zulu origin) — implies it is the origin point of the continent. Contributes to Cindermarch's weather pattern: snow to the north, clear to the south.

continents.name: Yetgrese
continents.flair: Fantastical in every way — should never feel like a standard fantasy setting. The geology is wrong, the demographics are wrong, the cities don't work like Kaemahz cities. Arriving here should feel like the rules changed.
continents.description: Second continent. 2-3 weeks sailing from Kaemahz's western coast; under 2 weeks with magical propulsion if crossing goes smoothly.
continents.climate: Variable regionally. Interior sea climate likely distinct from exterior coasts due to geological shelter.

geography.shape: Crescent — massive partial crater or caldera, eroded asymmetrically over millennia
geography.western: Massive, mountainous, intact. Tallest and most dramatic terrain. Volcanic or meteoric origin — meteoric preferred, TBD.
geography.eastern: Partially eroded and broken. Lower elevation. Where the old crater wall wore away.
geography.gap: Open waterway where the eastern wall eroded through — connects outer ocean to interior sea.
geography.interior_sea: Massively deep. Geologically sheltered and isolated for millennia. Likely contains unique fauna. Mostly cliffed borders with no beaches — cliffs grow dramatically taller moving west.
geography.archipelago: Complex island chain in the interior where the eroded eastern face crumbled into the water over millennia. Remnants of the old crater wall.
geography.target_city: On the eastern face of the main continent, slightly north of the waterway gap, facing outward toward the open sea.

demographics.notes: Humans are 15-20% of population at most. Several familiar races present but as less common or divergent subtypes — not standard Kaemahz versions. Full demographic composition still being established. Do not default to human NPCs.

continents.notes: Dangerous crossing — weather, distance, and navigation all factors. Difficult enough that most Kaemahz residents have never met anyone from there. Occasional traders make the crossing. Target city is trade-accessible but not frequently visited — arrival is noteworthy but not unprecedented.

continents.name: Senkolai
continents.flair: a continent that is a single living thing — one impossibly old, impossibly large clonal tree-organism with five surviving trunks, and a civilization that has spent longer building inside it than most nations spend existing. Culture here is stratified by altitude, not geography. Your nation isn't which country you were born in — it's which band of the tree you were born on.
continents.draft_note: this is a from-scratch continent proposal, built overnight for review — nothing here is canon yet. Read it, keep what's useful, discard or rewrite the rest with no ceremony required. Built deliberately against the grain of both known continents: no lateral map-of-nations like Kaemahz's seven regions, and no crater/interior-sea geology like Yetgrese's. Different axis entirely — this one is organized by height, not by border.
continents.description:
Far south of Solvale with treacherous waters and shifting currents between and a vast distance means no one in Kaemahz is aware it exists.

There is no native word for the continent as a whole. None of the five Boles consider themselves part of a shared landmass-identity — each regards itself as the center, and the others as neighbors at best, curiosities at worst. "Senkolai" will be its name for this document. Each of the five boles and each of the vertical levels have their own names.
continents.the_everbole:
The whole concept: it's one organism. What looks, from a ship's deck, like five separate sky-scratching trees — to be one continuous root system, feeding five above-ground trunks (the Boles) that have grown independently for so long they no longer resemble each other, share no aboveground connection, and would be classified as different species entirely if anyone tried. They are the same living thing. Insiders call it the Everbole (name pending), when they call it anything — most people below Kelmoth just call it "the root," lowercase, the way you'd refer to weather.

Its age is unknown and unknowable by any method locals have. Its lower trunk sections — the mid-height mass that the Mistbelt and much of the Root Deep are built in and on — are no longer properly alive in the way the crown is: they petrified into a stone-wood hybrid material over some unfathomable span, dense and workable like fine-grained granite but grained like heartwood, called stonewood (name pending) locally. The crown canopy at the top is still fully, riotously alive. The deep root tangle at the very bottom is alive too, and still slowly growing, still slowly searching — for what, if anything, nobody who lives there claims to know, though the deepest root miners have opinions they don't share with outsiders. The mines are accessible through shaft 'dug' in the petrified wood near the water and must remain in the interior of the trees protection until reaching stone below surface. Any miscalculated strike results in a flood of seawater that must be dangerously repaired or the shaft abandoned.

This means the continent's "geology" is actually anatomy. What Kaemahz would call a mountain range is the Everbole's fossilized trunk-mass. What would be called a cave system is stonewood heartwood, hollowed by insects, water, and centuries of deliberate excavation. There is no volcanism here, no tectonic drama — the closest thing to a natural disaster is a limb-fall (or an ocean storm), when an aging crown branch the size of a small kingdom's forest finally lets go and comes down through the lower bands, which is exactly as catastrophic and as survivable-with-warning as it sounds, and which every Bole has a different name for and a different set of rituals around.

geography.overview: Every one of the five Boles is internally divided into the same three vertical bands — this is the real cultural map of Senkolai, cutting across Bole identity the way a social class might cut across a Kaemahz kingdom. A Canopy-dweller from Sennar and a Canopy-dweller from Kelmoth have more in common with each other, culturally, than either does with the Root Deep two miles straight down in their own Bole. This shared cultural divide hints at a more unified people in ages past.

bands.The Reach: (bad name, needs changed) (canopy, top band) — the living crown, kilometers of interwoven branch-mass thick enough to build on, with settlements strung across branch-forks and grown-lattice platforms rather than cleared ground. Full sun, constant wind, near-constant vertigo for anyone not raised in it. Settlements are light, rope-and-platform construction that flexes with the wind rather than fighting it — a Reach building that doesn't sway in a storm is considered badly built, not well built. Population here skews toward folk with some means of not falling: aarakocra communities are the oldest established presence, alongside tabaxi who favor the branch-running life, and a long-adapted human lineage — Reach-born humans, no different in stock (mmm, maybe no humans here) from anyone in Kaemahz but raised from infancy on platforms with gaps, and famous (or notorious, depending who's asked) among lowlanders for an essentially nonexistent fear of heights and a corresponding total inability to sleep well indoors on solid ground.
bands.The Shroud: (mistbelt, middle band) (doesn't make sense to be the middle band, it would block sun from the lower band; tree canopy would also, so unless we want the lower band to be really dark all the time this might needed changedd) — a near-permanent fog layer where the living crown gives way to the petrified stonewood trunk-mass beneath it, thick enough that direct sunlight is a rumor and most navigation is done by sound, smell, and the bioluminescent fungal colonies that carpet every horizontal stonewood surface. Culturally the most inward-facing of the three bands — the fog discourages both casual travel and casual conquest, and Shroud settlements have historically just... not needed doors that lock, because nobody comes through who wasn't already meant to be there. Firbolgs are the dominant folk here, alongside gnomes who took to fungal cultivation and bioluminescent artifice with real enthusiasm, and a small, quiet human lineage that's adapted toward genuinely excellent low-light vision over generations rather than any magical means anyone can point to.
bands.The Root Deep: (bottom band) — the excavated stonewood heartwood and the true earth beneath it, where the trunk gives way to the still-living, still- searching root tangle. Warmer than the bands above (something about the Everbole's own slow metabolism), tunnel-built rather than platform-built, and the most socially rigid of the three bands — lineage matters enormously here, in a way it doesn't above, because a family's claim to a particular seam of stonewood or root-cavity is inherited property, defended for generations. Goliaths adapted to tunnel life rather than open sky are the oldest confirmed presence, working alongside deep gnomes and tortles, whose shells and temperament suit slow, patient stonewood excavation unusually well. Root Deep folk regard both bands above them with something between pity and contempt — "unrooted," in the local idiom, is not a compliment.

boles.Kelmoth: the oldest and largest trunk, and by informal but nearly universal consent, the center: not a capital (nothing here has a capital in the Kaemahz sense), but the site of the Everbole's oldest confirmed growth and the place every band's religious tradition agrees is spiritually significant, even though they disagree about almost everything else. Home to the Concord of the Root — not a government, a gathering, held on no fixed schedule (the last one was eleven years ago; the one before that, thirty-four) at a specific ring-platform where all three bands physically meet, called only when a dispute or a discovery is judged too large for one Bole to sit on alone. Whichever band hosts the current Concord provides the location; the ring-platform itself belongs to none of them.
boles.Sennar: the Reach at its most developed: the largest sky-trade hub on the continent, the closest thing Senkolai has to a "capital of the air," and the Bole most likely to have heard of Kaemahz at all, thanks to a trickle of glider-borne trade with Halcoro. Loud, confident, and unbothered by height in a way that unsettles every visitor from solid ground.
boles.Dolkren: the Root Deep's stronghold, the most insular and lineage- bound of the five, and the source of nearly all worked stonewood that ever leaves the continent. Outsiders are tolerated here for exactly as long as a trade transaction requires and not one hour longer. Dolkren miners are the only people on Senkolai who have ever, on record, broken through into open space beneath the deepest confirmed root-mass — a handful of times, always sealed back up immediately, always described afterward in the same word across unrelated mining families who'd never spoken to each other: wrong.
boles.Ozhmerel: the Shroud's deepest expression, wrapped almost entirely in permanent fog even by mistbelt standards, and home to the Listening Silence, a religious-scholarly order that spends careers learning to hear the Everbole's own sap-pulse and treats what it hears as scripture in progress rather than fixed doctrine. Quietest place on the continent, by design and by culture, not by lack of population.
boles.Halcoro: the youngest Bole (a relative term — still centuries old), the least internally consistent, and the only real point of contact with the outside world. Its Root Deep meets tidal river-delta where the Everbole's roots finally reach salt water, in a brackish mangrove sprawl called the Rootmouth — the one place on Senkolai with a functioning, Kaemahz-recognizable port. Humans are the plurality here, not because they dominate anywhere else on the continent but because Halcoro is where outsiders, refugees, and anyone who didn't fit cleanly into a Reach, Shroud, or Root Deep identity elsewhere have been drifting for generations. If Senkolai ever produces a diplomat, a translator, or a ship Kaemahz has heard of, they're from Halcoro.

geography.windscar: Past the edge of the Everbole's root-reach, where the ground stops being part of the organism at all, the land breaks into a wind-scoured plain the locals call the Windscar — the one part of Senkolai that would look almost familiar to a Kaemahz traveler, except for the wind, which does not stop, ever, and shapes everything from the architecture (there isn't much) to the culture (thoroughly nomadic) to the local wildlife (large, low, and built to not get picked up). The Windscar clans ride tamed windhawks — condor-sized, sail-winged, genuinely dangerous animals that a rider spends a decade earning the trust of — and treat the Everbole's people as strange, sedentary, slightly pitiable cousins, which is an opinion returned with equal enthusiasm in the other direction. Genasi (air-touched, mostly) and hardy human lineages make up the clans in roughly even measure; nobody keeps a census, since a census requires people to stay in one place long enough to be counted.

continents.demographics: No single species or lineage dominates Senkolai the way humans anchor Kaemahz or dragonborn concentrate in its south. Roughly: aarakocra and Reach-adapted humans in the canopy; firbolgs, gnomes, and low-light-adapted humans in the mistbelt; goliaths, deep gnomes, and tortles in the root deep; air genasi and windrider humans on the Windscar; and everyone, in whatever proportion currently holds, in Halcoro. Dwarves and dragonborn exist here but only as rare individual travelers or transplants — neither has an established community, and that's worth preserving rather than "fixing," since both already anchor other parts of the setting.

religion.overview: There is no pantheon here, personified or otherwise — nothing like Tellonde's Greek-with-twists gods, and nothing like Fol's spirit-shamanism either, though it shares Fol's instinct that the divine is a present, physical thing rather than a distant one. What's venerated is the Everbole itself, and — this is the load-bearing detail — the three bands disagree, sincerely and without much rancor, about what happens to a person when they die, and the disagreement maps exactly onto the vertical geography:

afterlives.The Reach: The Reach holds that a spirit rises — that dying properly means ascending past the crown entirely, and that Reach funeral rites (a body released from the highest platform available, weighted with nothing) are designed to give the spirit the cleanest possible path upward.
afterlives.The Root Deep: The Root Deep holds the mirror belief: that a spirit descends, returning to and feeding the root tangle that fed it in life, which is why root-deep burial is literal — a body worked back into a claimed root-cavity, becoming part of the family's inherited ground.
afterlives.The Shroud: The Shroud, in between both geographically and theologically, holds that a spirit does neither — that it lingers, becoming part of the fog itself, neither rising nor descending, which is the belief the Listening Silence in Ozhmerel has built an entire scholarly tradition around: if the dead linger in the mist, then the mist can, in principle, be listened to.

religion.closing: None of the three bands considers the others heretical, exactly — more like each thinks the others are describing a different, smaller truth. A Reach funeral held for a Root Deep-born spouse is a genuine diplomatic occasion, handled the way an interfaith wedding might be handled elsewhere.

continents.magic_and_sap_tide:
Primal and druidic traditions are the load-bearing magic of Senkolai in a way arcane wizardry simply isn't — a traveling Kaemahz wizard is treated with the mild, polite bewilderment of someone practicing a craft everyone agrees is clever but nobody quite sees the point of, when the Everbole itself is right there to work with instead. Druids, primal casters, and the Listening Silence's sap-readers hold the cultural position clerics and wizards split between them in Kaemahz.

Layered on top of Tellonde's base calendar (the same 204-day year, four 51-day seasons, that governs the rest of the known world) is a purely local rhythm: the sap-tide, a roughly 17-day cycle — about three per season, a little over a dozen a year — during which the Everbole's sap visibly rises through the whole structure. During a Tide, the crown flushes with new color, Shroud bioluminescence intensifies until the fog itself seems to glow, root-deep tunnels warm perceptibly, and climbing or traveling with the grain of the trunk gets measurably easier — several druidic and primal effects are locally held (and, per the Listening Silence's records, reliably observed) to work better during a Tide. Between Tides is the Still — drier, quieter, harder climbing, but the best working conditions for Dolkren's stonewood miners, since the receded sap exposes seams a Tide would hide. Any Senkolai native can tell you without thinking which phase the continent is currently in; it's as unremarkable and as load-bearing to them as knowing the time of day.
continents.trade_and_export: Senkolai's exports are valuable specifically because nothing else produces them: stonewood (Dolkren's worked stone-grain heartwood, strong and fine enough for tool and weapon hafts that never warp); heartglass (rare naturally-formed clear amber-like petrified sap, prized by artificers and jewelers for lenses and inlay, found only in old stonewood seams and already commanding absurd prices in the one or two Kaemahz ports that have seen a sample); bioluminescent fungal cultures from the Shroud, which survive transplant surprisingly well and are quietly becoming a novelty lighting trade in coastal Kaemahz cities; and windhawk feathers from the Windscar clans, who trade them reluctantly and only through Halcoro intermediaries, since parting with a feather from a living, bonded bird is a genuine cultural taboo and most trade feathers come from natural molt or a bird's death of old age.

naming_conventions.overview: Kept distinct per band deliberately, since the bands don't consider themselves one culture:

by_culture.Reach names: flowing, vowel-heavy, often built from compounded wind/light/height concepts, frequently using an apostrophe to mark a glottal stop between vowel clusters. Soft consonants only (l, n, m, r, s, y, h) — no hard stops. Examples: Sennar, Aelu'nar, Yothrelin, Sai'omeh.
by_culture.Shroud names: soft, sibilant, whisper-register — sh/zh, f, s, th sounds dominate, words tend short. Examples: Ozhmerel, Shuvenn, Fenzashi.
by_culture.Root Deep names: short, hard, percussive, built on consonant clusters (kr, dr, gn, str) and closed syllables — the opposite instinct from Reach naming entirely. Examples: Dolkren, Krast, Gundrek, Ovrik.
by_culture.Windscar names: clan-based rather than place-based, since there are no fixed settlements to name — a clan is named for the storm it was founded under or the windhawk lineage it rides, in blunt descriptive compounds. Examples: Redgale Clan, the Duskhowl Riders, Longwing Clan.
by_culture.Halcoro names: deliberately inconsistent — a trade-pidgin blend of all three band-languages plus borrowed Kaemahz fragments. The inconsistency is the convention; a "proper" Halcoro name is one that sounds like it came from nowhere in particular.

naming_conventions.avoid: any -march/-wald/-vath/-vale/-dal suffix pattern (heavily used across Kaemahz already), a Tor- prefix (flagged overused there too), and V-heavy names generally (Fol's tribes already lean hard on that sound).

mysteries_and_hooks: What's beneath the roots. Dolkren's rare breakthroughs into open space under the deepest confirmed root-mass are real, on record, and unexplained. "Wrong" is the only word that survives every independent account. Nobody has stayed down there long enough to describe it further. Left deliberately open, same spirit as Yetgrese's crater origin and Kaemahz's Orvath teleport circle — a hook, not an answer.

Whether the Everbole is aware. No consensus, even among the Listening Silence, on whether the organism they've built a religion around has anything like a mind, or whether the sap-pulse is just biology being mistaken for meaning. A visiting skeptic and a lifelong believer would have a genuinely unresolved argument, not a "the DM knows and one side is just wrong" argument.

The next limb-fall. Every Bole tracks warning signs (canopy stress, sap-tide irregularities) differently, and a limb-fall large enough to hit more than one Bole at once has apparently never happened in living memory — which either means it can't, or means nobody's been watching long enough yet.

First real contact. Nothing here assumes Senkolai has ever sent anyone to Kaemahz, or vice versa, successfully and repeatably — the Halcoro trade trickle is thin and one-directional so far. A party being the first documented round trip is entirely on the table.
connections: Kaemahz — the far side of the Vastreach crossing.
Yetgrese — the other known continent; unrelated to Senkolai by geography or theme, noted here only as the existing point of contrast this draft was written against.

name: Fynesmarch
flair: The working coast — trade, ships, and the friction between old money and new ambition. Cities feel economically motivated rather than heroic. People here are trying to get ahead, stay out of trouble, or both. The most grounded region in Kaemahz.
climate: Temperate maritime overall, distinct microclimates city to city.
shape_note: Wide and shallow — twice as far east-west as north-south.
naming_conventions: Literal and descriptive. Place names directly reflect observable features — Cindermarch is a fortress (march) near ashen terrain from the Inkaba volcano. This pattern should guide generation of new place names consistently.
notes: Primary campaign region. Cindermarch on its northeastern border served as a fortress during past conflict with Fol — that conflict has ended. Cindermarch is now both a fortress and a functioning city.

name: Fol
flair: A land where iron is sacred and shamanism is the architecture of the world. Entering Fol feels like stepping into an older, more coherent logic — one that works, just not in any way a Kaemahz merchant would recognize. The spirits are not metaphors here.
culture: Tribal and shamanistic. Ironworking is culturally central — not merely a trade skill but an identity, bound up in spiritual practice. Shamanism is the primary spiritual framework. No merchant-council structure, no capital.

known: Veratha — known as the Firstwalkers. The name implies a belief that they were the first people to walk the land, potentially predating other civilizations on Kaemahz.
tribes.notes: Avoid generating more V-names for new tribes in this region.

sub_regions.name: Northern Cliffs
sub_regions.description: Cliff-faced coastline, no sea access, harsh winters, no sailing culture.

notes: Past conflict with Fynesmarch has ended. Cindermarch fortress exists due to historical raids, not active conflict.
shape_notes: Top point (20,40) — furthest north. Top left coast (20,40) to (0,20). Top right coast (20,40) to (40,20). Bottom left border (0,20) to (8,0). Bottom right border (40,20) to (32,0). Bottom edge (8,0) to (32,0) — Fynesmarch border.

locations.name: Cindermarch
locations.description: Bottom center on border line. Military fortress, Fynesmarch side.

locations.name: Northern Rock Waystation
locations.description: Rock overhang shelter. Firstwalker songs carved in hearthstone.

locations.name: Vethara Winter Camp
locations.description: Northeast of Cindermarch. Firstwalker winter camp.

locations.name: Greyspine Passage
locations.description: Narrow mountain passage. Only winter route through the ridge.

locations.name: Observatory
locations.description: Ancient pre-settlement structure. Mast's research base.

name: Torwald
flair: Proud, self-aware, and slightly insufferable about it. Torwald is what happens when a culture survives an empire without being touched by it — and then keeps the original form so carefully that it starts to calcify. Still vital, still impressive. Just very sure of itself, and not entirely wrong to be.
culture: Anglo-Saxon cultural feel. Considers itself the keeper of original culture — both its own and what Aranwald set aside. Slightly smug about this. Never occupied by Solvale.
relationship_with_aranwald: Familial and good overall, with a persistent tension. Torwald finds Aranwald's embrace of Solvaran aesthetics gauche — sees it as celebrating the style of an occupier. Torwald views itself as the keeper of what both kingdoms once were; Aranwald regards this position as provincial.
history: Once a single kingdom with what is now Aranwald. The Solvale Empire occupied the southern half for approximately 200 years, effectively splitting the territory. A prince eventually recaptured the occupied territory and renamed it Aranwald, formalizing the split. A sibling on the Torwald side was reportedly indignant about not being the one to recapture it — the kingdoms separated formally but retained familial connection. See Aranwald for the full account.
naming_conventions: Torwald settlements are named for lineage rather than geography. A place is named for whoever claimed it — a founding family, a clan elder, an early explorer — using a possessive or clan-suffix construction. Over generations the possessive erodes into a single fused word, so a settlement founded as 'Dunric's Hold' or similar becomes simply Dunric. The name preserves an ownership claim long after anyone remembers who originally held it. HOW TO notes: Take a personal name (2-3 syllables, hard consonants, Northern/Highland phonetic character) and fuse it with a shortened place-word or suffix rather than keeping them as two separate words. Favor hard endings — consonant clusters, -ric, -cavel, -mark constructions — over soft vowel endings. The result should feel like it used to be a full possessive phrase and has been worn smooth by generations of use. Avoid Tor- as a prefix; it is heavily overused in this world's existing naming pool. Examples already established: Dunric (pass), Duncavel (town) — implying both places trace to the same original claimant or clan, 'Dun-.'

name: Aranwald
flair: A kingdom that was occupied for two centuries, fought back, and then chose to keep the art, the architecture, and the aesthetic of the occupier — because they beat them, and that means it belongs to them now. The most stylistically layered region in Kaemahz. Conquest here is something you metabolize.
culture: Persian-Anglo fusion. Occupied by the Solvale Empire for approximately 200 years. A prince recaptured it and coined the name deliberately — kept 'wald' for continuity with the land, replaced 'Tor' with 'Aran' (Persian: peaceful/noble). Founding philosophy: 'we didn't just conquer the land, we conquered everything.' Solvaran artifacts, architecture, and cultural elements are high-status symbols — trophies of strength, not shameful remnants. Solvaran scholars and craftsmen increasingly emigrating here as the empire destabilizes.
solvaran_cultural_inheritance: The occupation left a deep imprint that Aranwald has deliberately reclaimed rather than erased: domed buildings and arched courtyards, elaborate geometric gardens, rich textiles and ornate metalwork, a strong poetry and oral tradition, possible fire worship or fire-adjacent religious practice, a taste for court intrigue, and a sophisticated bureaucratic tradition. These elements are visible throughout Feldtazur's architecture and the aristocratic culture of the region.
relationship_with_torwald: Familial and good overall. Aranwald regards Torwald's insistence on pre-Solvaran tradition as provincial — clinging to what was rather than mastering what is. Both views are stated with family fondness rather than hostility.
split_history: Torwald and Aranwald were once a single kingdom. The Solvale Empire's occupation of the southern half lasted approximately 200 years before a prince recaptured the territory and renamed it Aranwald, breaking formal unity permanently. A sibling on the Torwald side was reportedly indignant about not being the hero of that moment. The kingdoms split but retained familial connection. The naming of Aranwald was a deliberate philosophical act, not merely a geographic one.
notes: Capital name Feldtazur coined by the prince — Anglo 'feld' + Persian-derived 'tazur'.
naming_conventions: Place names mix Anglo, Gaelic and Persian/North African roots (Feldtazur, Hallamar, Bethasan, Qalmarrow).
border_with_torwald: Near Feldtazur the border is crossed by unmarked boundary stones carved with a defaced eagle, and a drover's track skips the toll-house.

name: Orvath
flair: A question-free banking haven in the middle of a high desert. Coming here means you have something to hide, something to protect, or you are trying to move money that other places would scrutinize. The city does not judge. That is the entire point, and it shapes everything from the architecture to the way strangers greet each other.
climate: High desert. Significant temperature variance between day and night. These conditions affect the magical weave differently than coastal or temperate regions — permanent magical structures require additional anchoring work. A teleportation circle established here approximately twenty years ago by an unknown practitioner functioned for four months then disappeared entirely, described as having 'gone somewhere else.' No permanent circle is known to exist in Orvath.
culture: Primarily elven population. Mongolian-inspired — nomadic heritage expressed in a settled city, clan-based social structure, horse culture adapted to desert context. Question-free banking is the defining feature to outsiders.
geography:
Mountains ring the region close enough in places that the horizon feels cropped — no long fade-to-blue of open plains here, just a hard wall of rock that goes gold to violet to black in about twenty minutes at dusk, under a night sky so undiluted by haze or lowland moisture that first-time visitors reportedly lose their footing looking up at it.

The oasis and its runoff (the same oasis the city of Orvath is built around) braid down through the foothills in threads, and where the water reaches, it reaches generously — not jungle-green, but the deep, disciplined green of terraced barley and stone-walled orchards clinging to slopes that shouldn't support them, tended by people who've spent centuries arguing with gravity and winning. A half-day's ride from that same terrace, the ground turns to cracked pan and nothing grows at all. Both are Orvath. Neither apologizes for the other — that tension (fertile terrace vs. dead pan, settled bank vs. nomadic clan) is the region's real character, not a contradiction to resolve.

The air itself is thin enough to notice — visitors get short of breath on stairs and don't understand why until someone tells them, unkindly, to drink more water and stop talking so much. Fuel is dung-brick and juniper scrub, not wood, so every hearth smells faintly resinous underneath the smoke.
culture_details: Fermented mare's-milk spirit is the ceremonial drink — offered to guests as both hospitality and a small test of composure. How a stranger handles it is read as character information.

Mounted archery is the region's signature skill, and a demanding one: bows are laminated from horn, sinew, and sarnach bone specifically because ordinary wood cracks under the day-to-night temperature swing. It's a bowyer's craft that takes decades to be trusted with, taught as much through feel as instruction. An archer who can shoot at a full gallop across broken ground at altitude, in air too thin for anyone untrained to breathe steadily, is not a generalist — everyone worth knowing here does one thing, and does it terrifyingly well.
Falconry, via the Sarnach, isn't a leisure pursuit here — it's load-bearing infrastructure the whole settled economy depends on.
dm_hooks: The vanished teleportation circle — already an established open hook, unrelated to duskglass mechanically (the circle failed despite presumably being built with proper anchoring), but worth keeping in the same mental bucket: Orvath's weave does something nobody fully understands yet.

What happens to the bank if the duskglass supply is ever seriously disrupted — a large storm-strike claimed by force instead of found fairly, a clan war over a big vein, a rival power trying to corner the supply to threaten the vaults' integrity. Not seeded yet; a strong lever for a banking-secrecy plot.

How banking neutrality was actually established and is maintained (the banking note on this entry also flags this as TBD) — duskglass explains why the vaults are physically possible here, not why depositors trust Orvath's discretion specifically. Separate open question, still worth developing.
banking: Anonymous deposits, no extradition, no questions asked — by design, not accident. The most secure financial institution on Kaemahz. How this status was established and maintained is TBD, but the implication is either significant political neutrality, deep historical precedent, or a power arrangement that makes interference more costly than cooperation.
notable: Contains an elderly cartographer considered the most knowledgeable living person on the eastern interior and territories beyond. He does not leave Orvath.
origin_notes: Physically possible because of duskglass — lightning-fused sand found only in Orvath's warped-weave conditions, the only substance that reliably anchors permanent magical structures here, and what the Banking Institution's vaults are built on. Harvested by the region's nomadic clans after storms (spotted via trained sarnach raptors), which is why they hold real leverage over the settled city rather than existing on its margins. See the lore entry "duskglass-001" for the full picture. Still open: how banking *neutrality/secrecy* specifically was established and is maintained — duskglass explains the vaults, not the discretion.
notes: Contains only one city, also called Orvath. 6 days north/northeast of Argentveil overland.

name: Birindal
flair: Two cultures that realized they needed each other and built a partnership instead of a country. Coast and mountain operate by different rules, worship different values, and have never tried to merge — the trade flows between them precisely because neither wants what the other has, only what the other produces.
culture: Two distinct communities maintain separate but cooperative identities. Coastal (Drinaell): Celtic/Nordic seafaring culture — merchant marine and raiding heritage, community governance by harbor council or similar. Mountain (Brakvunder): Dwarven stronghold culture — deep craft tradition, independent governance, minimal interest in maritime affairs.
governance: No capital because the coastal and mountain communities govern themselves independently. No central authority both sides would accept — and neither has pushed for one. The arrangement works because their needs are complementary rather than competitive.
drinaell_brakvunder_relationship: Maritime trade partnership. Brakvunder produces metal, stone, and finished craft goods; Drinaell moves them. Drinaell provides sea access and external trade networks; Brakvunder provides inland security and resources. How Drinaell became the dominant maritime force on Kaemahz is TBD — likely geography, shipbuilding tradition, and absence of strong competition from other regions.

name: Solvale
flair: The bones of a great empire with not enough people left to fill them. The architecture is still extraordinary. The cultural sophistication is still real. But the city was built for twice its current population and the scale of the emptiness is its own kind of statement. Beautiful and melancholy in equal measure.
climate: Warm to tropical, North African/Moroccan feel.
culture: Once the heart of the Solvale Empire — still uses the imperial name. People are called Solvaran. At its height: architecturally stunning, culturally sophisticated, center of learning and trade. Cultural exports — art, poetry, bureaucratic method, architectural style — shaped Aranwald for generations of occupation.
collapse: The empire extracted Aranwald's resources for approximately 200 years, then lost it. The entire economic engine collapsed without that resource base. Dictatorial leadership that had built the empire proved unable to adapt — the same structures that enabled expansion prevented recovery.
current_state: Yshavar is now a city built for more people than inhabit it. Public buildings maintained by habit more than necessity. The grandeur is still visible — the bones of empire are impressive — but the scale no longer matches the population.
notes: Southernmost region of Kaemahz. A recovery path exists but is politically nearly impossible without outside intervention or significant leadership change. Potential campaign arc.
